grades.quote: The process ID remains the same because `execl` has changed what program the process is running without changing the process itself.
grades.reason: Explains that exec replaces the program in the same process without changing the process (same PID, no return on success). This is background on exec, but it never says why a shell forks first.

grades.quote: A common example is fork followed by exec: a few pages may be written after the fork, but then the child’s exec releases the bulk of the memory inherited from the parent.
grades.reason: Covers COW fork and mentions the fork-then-exec pattern, where exec releases the memory the child inherited. This is auxiliary. It does not explain why a shell forks before exec.

grades.quote: The child process creates a pipe to connect the left end of the pipeline with the right end. Then it calls fork and runcmd for the left end of the pipeline and fork and runcmd for the right end, and waits for both to finish.
grades.reason: Shows the xv6 shell forking a child that then runs exec, and the shell waits for its children. It does not explicitly say why the shell doesn't exec directly, so it only gives limited related context.

grades.quote: This happens, for example, every time you type a program’s name at a shell prompt; the shell forks off a child process in which it runs the program.
grades.reason: Says that a common use of fork is creating a child to run a different program, as the shell does whenever you type a command. It also says exec loads a new program into the calling process. Together these imply the shell forks so that it survives. It does not state the "shell would be replaced" reasoning outright.
